source.title: Scaling Laws for Fine-Grained Mixture of Experts
source.authors: Jakub Krajewski; Jan Ludziejewski; Kamil Adamczewski; Maciej Pi'oro; Michal Krutul; Szymon Antoniak; Kamil Ciebiera; Krystian Kr'ol; Tomasz Odrzyg'o'zd'z; Piotr Sankowski; Marek Cygan; Sebastian Jaszczur

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. The reported scaling fits use smoothed training loss, not held-out loss.
record.tranche_reason: The paper fits scaling laws for fine-grained MoE and reports how fitted coefficients and compute-optimal configurations vary with architecture and expansion rate. This refines the scope of scaling-law claims rather than reproducing the original dense-model studies.
record.gate_note: The study reports fitted loss laws and compute-optimal configurations for decoder-only models trained on C4. It describes the loss used for analysis as smoothed training loss. Cited scaling-law findings from other studies are not recorded as results. The paper also reports a wall-clock comparison for G=8 versus G=16, but that timing result does not itself measure any listed claim version.
record.test_reason: The study fits Chinchilla-form power laws in N and D, plus a granularity term, to over 100 fine-grained MoE language-model runs and to dense runs on C4. It checks fit quality and hold-out validation, then derives compute-optimal N and D. This is a new architectural setting with results on V1, V2, V3 and V7. It is not a refutation of any version, so T3 fits better than T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that the authors claim the MoE–dense efficiency gap widens with scale (20× at 1e20 FLOPs, over 40× past 1e25), contrary to Clark et al. Add that this follows from letting training tokens vary.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops and fits a joint scaling law for MoE with a granularity variable, then optimizes MoE configurations under a compute budget. It uses smoothed training loss and C4 experiments, rather than reproducing the original dense-model measurement procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported fitted coefficients vary between E=64 and E=16 and between dense and MoE fits. The authors also note that very high granularity can reduce performance and increase routing cost.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed N and D, loss falls as a power law in expert granularity G toward a constant. Very high G (64 at dmodel=256) degrades performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MoE language-model loss follows a power law in expert granularity, with gains bounded by routing overhead at extreme granularity.

fits_no_version.finding: Compute-optimal MoE is predicted to match dense Transformers at 20× less compute at 1e20 FLOPs, rising past 40× beyond 1e25 FLOPs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The compute efficiency gap between optimally configured MoE and dense Transformers widens with training budget.

record.problems: The analyzed loss is smoothed training loss rather than held-out loss. The models used for the main fits range from 129M to 3.7B parameters, and the paper does not validate predictions on runs orders of magnitude larger. Compute-optimal configurations are derived from fitted laws and specified FLOPs assumptions; the authors note that actual training costs depend on hardware and implementation. The E=16 study uses fewer experiments and shorter training durations, with wider bootstrap intervals.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant reported result rows omitted. The paper's wall-clock example for G=8 versus G=16 is mentioned in gate_note because it does not measure a listed claim version.

untested.parts: Held-out loss (smoothed training loss is used, in a no-repeat regime). Range spans only about 1.5 orders in N and under 1 order in D.
Prediction of runs orders of magnitude larger. The Table 2 configurations up to 64×1T are not trained.
No power-law exponents are fitted for N_opt and D_opt versus compute. The optima are not validated by trained runs.
Not tested. The paper assumes dmodel=64·nblocks, citing Kaplan's finding on depth-to-width ratio.
Not tested. Only text pretraining on C4, with no other modalities, repeated data or fine-tuning.
Training schedule, parameter counting, data and fitting-method alternatives are not varied. No curvature away from a power law is examined.

missing.what: Joint-fit RMSE 0.015, and the power law in N and D at fixed G (V1 evidence).
Bootstrap 10th–90th percentiles for E=64 optimal D and G, e.g. 64×1T D=(5.29T,16.87T).
The benefit of more training tokens is nearly independent of G, which justifies the shared β.

record.verdict_notes: The source does not support the record's T5 tranche; T3 is used. V1 is re-scored as tested: training loss in a no-repeat regime, following Hoffmann, is a reasonable proxy, but the caveat is labelled. All compute-optimal rows are model-derived extrapolations, not trained runs. The dense fit's exponents (about 0.13) differ sharply from Chinchilla's, which may bear on V7, but the paper does not discuss it.

versions.untested_parts: The paper fits smoothed training loss, not held-out pretraining loss.
Validation excludes the 20% of models with the lowest perplexity, but does not test predictions on runs orders of magnitude larger than the fitted runs.

The paper optimizes MoE configurations, including granularity, rather than testing the dense-model alternatives in the claim. It gives compute-optimal configurations at selected budgets but does not fit a power-law exponent for each of optimal parameter count and token count.
Architecture depth and width are not varied to test their effect on loss at fixed parameter count.
The experiments concern text pretraining on C4; other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
The paper compares some architectural and expansion-rate choices, but does not systematically vary all fitting choices, data, or training schedules named in the version.

relationships.condition: MoE optima versus Hoffmann et al.'s equal-growth version; E=16 bootstrap
relationships.reason: Tokens per active parameter fall from about 44 (64×100M) to about 8 (64×1T), so N grows faster than D (R6–R12). The authors say this matches Hoffmann only around 1B–10B. E=16 intervals span up to about 8× in D (R17–R19).
relationships.display_finding: Tokens per active parameter fell from about 44 to 8, matching Hoffmann only around 1B–10B; E=16 intervals spanned up to about 8× in tokens.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: MoE optima versus Hoffmann et al.'s equal-growth version; E=16 bootstrap
source_check.reason: R6–R12 predict decreasing tokens per active parameter, qualifying equal-growth allocation within this fitted optimizer. Table 2 restricts approximate agreement with Hoffmann to 1B–10B active parameters; R17–R19 show broad predicted intervals.

relationships.condition: Dense versus MoE, and E=64 versus E=16
relationships.reason: Fitted exponents shift with architecture and setup: β is 0.127 for dense vs 0.147 for MoE, and γ is 0.58 at E=64 vs 0.986 at E=16 (R2–R4). The compute-optimal split also differs.
relationships.display_finding: The exponent β is 0.127 for dense models versus 0.147 for MoE, γ is 0.58 at E=64 versus 0.986 at E=16, and optimal compute allocation also differs.
